$comment: The specification of contract §5's inscription filter, and the one place its two implementations meet.

§5 requires markup, scripts, URLs, bare domain names, email addresses and telephone numbers stripped 'at entry and again at render'. Those are two passes in two runtimes: the entry pass runs in the backend at issuance (backend/src/modules/deal/inscription.ts), because the endpoint carrying an inscription — POST /store/carts/:id — is public and accepts arbitrary metadata, so a filter in the checkout form filters nothing; the render pass runs in the storefront (storefront/src/lib/inscription.ts), because §5 also requires an operator to be able to blank an inscription later without reissuing the certificate, which is only possible if the rendered document is derived every time.

There is no package shared between the two workspaces — the backend emits CommonJS under ts-node and the storefront is ESM under Next — so there are two copies of the rules. This file is what stops them drifting: both test suites run every case below against their own implementation, and backend/tests/inscription-filter.test.ts additionally compares the two files' rule sections character for character.
'expected: null' means nothing survives and the certificate shows its no-inscription state, which §5 requires to look deliberate rather than truncated.
Cases marked 'gate' were found by a Gate D review of LD-09's V7 and are the reason the rules are shaped the way they are. Deleting one re-opens a defect somebody already found.

limits.$comment: §5 gives 120 for the dedication and calls the display name 'short'. 60 is C2's number, not the contract's: it is what fits the certificate's BEARER row on one line at 390px. Counted after filtering, not before.

cases.why: a bare domain with a path

a schemeless pseudo-URL is KEPT, and this is a decision rather than a gap: an inscription is rendered as text and never as an href or any attribute, so 'javascript:alert(1)' cannot execute anywhere it appears; §5's targets are a billboard and a phishing surface and this is neither; and the rule that would catch it — any word followed by a colon — eats 'Note:' and '10:30', which is the same over-eagerness three Gate D findings already punished
a script element and its body, not merely its tags
a style element and its body
markup around text keeps the text
the offending part goes and the rest stays
gate: a missing space after a full stop is a typing slip, not a domain
gate: a space-grouped quantity is arithmetic, not a telephone number
gate: an ISO date with a time is a date
collapses the whitespace a removal leaves behind
